heading: Engineering Trade-offs
subtitle: Not tech opinions — decisions, and the trade-offs accepted with them.

items.title: Kafka vs synchronous communication
items.question: When is an event bus worth the added complexity?
items.answer: When downstream consumers can tolerate eventual consistency and the producer shouldn't be blocked by, or coupled to, their availability. If the caller needs an immediate answer to proceed, a synchronous call is simpler and easier to reason about — the moment you need fan-out, replay or independent scaling of consumers, an event bus starts paying for itself.

items.title: SQL vs NoSQL
items.question: Why default to a relational database?
items.answer: Most business domains have relationships and invariants worth enforcing at the data layer, not just in application code. I reach for NoSQL when the access pattern is genuinely document- or key-based, when schema flexibility outweighs the value of constraints, or when horizontal write scale is the actual bottleneck — not by default.

items.title: Monolith vs microservices
items.question: When do microservices actually pay off?
items.answer: When independent teams need to deploy independently, or a specific component's scaling and reliability needs genuinely diverge from the rest of the system. Splitting a system before that pressure exists usually just trades one kind of complexity (a large codebase) for a worse one (distributed failure modes) without a matching benefit.

items.title: Cache vs database
items.question: What earns a cache instead of just hitting the database?
items.answer: Read-heavy, latency-sensitive paths where the data tolerates being slightly stale. The trade-off is always invalidation complexity, so I only add a cache once I can point at the specific query or endpoint that needs it, with a clear invalidation strategy already decided.

items.title: Consistency vs availability
items.question: How do you decide where a system sits on that spectrum?
items.answer: By asking what a stale or unavailable read actually costs in that specific domain. A financial transaction favors consistency even at the cost of availability during a partition; a product catalog favors availability, because a slightly outdated price is a smaller problem than the page failing to load.

items.title: REST vs event-driven
items.question: How do you choose between a request/response API and an event-driven flow?
items.answer: REST when a client needs a direct answer to a specific question. Event-driven when the goal is to notify multiple, decoupled consumers that something happened without the producer needing to know who's listening — the two usually coexist in the same system rather than compete.
